issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette:
Bao had always taken pride in his understanding of the human body-its resilience, its mechanics, its capacity for healing. As a physical therapist, this was his trade and his passion. But for the last eight months, since the rainy Tuesday when a panel van ran a red light, his own body had felt like a foreign and treacherous country. He remembered the moment with a sickening, fragmented clarity: not as a continuous story, but as a series of sensory snapshots. The squeal of tires on wet asphalt, the sudden, blinding glare of headlights through his passenger-side window, and the deafening, metallic roar as the world compressed around him. He'd woken up in the hospital with a shattered femur and three fractured ribs, his professional knowledge a source of cold comfort against the searing pain.

The physical recovery was arduous but, by all objective measures, successful. His colleagues praised his diligence with his own rehabilitation. His wife, Linh, celebrated each milestone. Yet, as his bones mended, his mind seemed to unravel. The world, once a predictable space, now felt riddled with hidden threats. Walking through the clinic where he worked, a place he once navigated with ease, became an exercise in threat assessment. He would find his eyes drawn to the heavy kettlebells lined up against the wall, no longer seeing them as tools for recovery but as blunt instruments. A dropped metal chart in the hallway would cause him to flinch violently, his heart hammering against his ribs as the sound of the impact echoed the crash. He began staying late after his last patient, not to finish notes, but to meticulously wipe down and rearrange every piece of equipment in his treatment room. The perfect alignment of weights, the sterile gleam of the parallel bars-this imposed order was the only thing that quieted the chaos in his head, if only for a little while.

At home, Linh noticed he was no longer present. He would be in the middle of a sentence and his focus would drift, his eyes scanning the room as if searching for an unseen danger. He couldn't concentrate on a movie, couldn't relax. He'd wake from nightmares drenched in sweat, the phantom sensation of being crushed still lingering in his limbs. He developed a ritual before they drove anywhere, mentally rehearsing a dozen different worst-case scenarios-a tire blowout on the freeway, a brake failure on a hill, another car appearing from nowhere. He believed this prepared him, but Linh just saw the tension coiling in his shoulders, his knuckles white on the steering wheel.

His work, his calling, suffered most. He had come to believe that his body was permanently damaged, a fragile thing that could betray him at any moment. This deep-seated conviction made it nearly impossible to trust himself with his patients. While demonstrating a simple lumbar stretch, he'd feel a twinge in his own back and be seized by the thought that his spine was about to give out. He could no longer trust his own physical intuition, the very sense that had made him a gifted therapist. Unwanted thoughts-the image of shattering glass, the memory of the paramedic's strained voice-would intrude while he was trying to count a patient's reps, leaving him disoriented and struggling to find his place. The confidence he once had in the body's ability to heal had been replaced by a profound fear of its vulnerability. He was certain he could no longer be trusted, that you could never truly know what might cause harm.

The breaking point came last week. He was helping an elderly woman regain her balance when a car backfired on the street outside the clinic's large window. Bao didn't just startle; he physically recoiled, letting go of the patient's support belt. She stumbled, catching herself on a nearby table, her face a mixture of fright and confusion. The shame was immediate and overwhelming. In that moment, he saw himself through her eyes: not a healer, but a source of instability and fear. It was the final piece of evidence that he was failing, that the accident had broken something inside him that physiotherapy couldn't fix. He came to therapy a week later, his voice low as he explained that he just wanted to feel solid in his own skin again, to be able to trust his own body enough to help others trust theirs.
